title: Reader’s digest version of scientific writing: comparative evaluation of summarization capacity between large language models and medical students in analyzing scientific writing in sleep medicine
abstract: Introduction As artificial intelligence systems like large language models (LLM) and natural language processing advance, the need to evaluate their utility within medicine and medical education grows. As medical research publications continue to grow exponentially, AI systems offer valuable opportunities to condense and synthesize information, especially in underrepresented areas such as Sleep Medicine. The present study aims to compare summarization capacity between LLM generated summaries of sleep medicine research article abstracts, to summaries generated by Medical Student (humans) and to evaluate if the research content, and literary readability summarized is retained comparably. Methods A collection of three AI-generated and human-generated summaries of sleep medicine research article abstracts were shared with 19 study participants (medical students) attending a sleep medicine conference. Participants were blind as to which summary was human or LLM generated. After reading both human and AI-generated research summaries participants completed a 1–5 Likert scale survey on the readability of the extracted writings. Participants also answered article-specific multiple-choice questions evaluating their comprehension of the summaries, as a representation of the quality of content retained by the AI-generated summaries. Results An independent sample t-test between the AI-generated and human-generated summaries comprehension by study participants revealed no significant difference between the Likert readability ratings (p = 0.702). A chi-squared test of proportions revealed no significant association (χ2 = 1.485, p = 0.223), and a McNemar test revealed no significant association between summary type and the proportion of correct responses to the comprehension multiple choice questions (p = 0.289). Discussion Some limitations in this study were a small number of participants and user bias. Participants attended at a sleep conference and study summaries were all from sleep medicine journals. Lastly the summaries did not include graphs, numbers, and pictures, and thus were limited in material extraction. While the present analysis did not demonstrate a significant difference among the readability and content quality between the AI and human-generated summaries, limitations in the present study indicate that more research is needed to objectively measure, and further define strengths and weaknesses of AI models in condensing medical literature into efficient and accurate summaries.

title: The DocLap integrated system for understanding multi-page scholarly documents
abstract: Computational understanding of documents is focused on visual and text analysis, building upon computer vision and natural language processing. With the advent of transformers document understanding is even more shifted from the actual comprehension of documents, which relies on concurrent perception of text, layout elements and document structure, to convoluted feature representations. Recent trends for providing unified access to such representations go towards Large Language Models (LLMs). However, these models have limitations: they lack explainability, demand significant resources for training and inference, and are not well suited for processing extensive inputs nor for direct application in specialized domains. This paper aims at creating a comprehensive interface for document analysis, enabling multi-layered exploration and integrating diverse features and contextual information. By bridging diverse information, our work pursues the identification, characterization, and linking of visual elements to semantic and contextual data, leveraging LLMs for interoperability. This enables a unified access to textual, visual, and structural layers, embedding levels of structured knowledge directly in the LLM context. Recent advances in Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) are also exploited to address some LLM limitations related to context length, allowing access to latent information from document representations such as graph and vector embeddings. The association of structural information to visual data allows formal analysis of documents and is exploited in our model to enhance visual recognition, improved through multi-modal LLM correction supported by ontology-based constraint violation detection. The framework enables semantic retrieval over extracted information, providing direct access to the document structure which can be exploited in many applications such as Question Answering (QA) and document understanding. As a result of this work, the DocLap (Document Layout Parser) system for document analysis and retrieval is proposed, which enables the extraction of visual and semantic features from documents and makes them accessible through natural language in an integrated framework providing conversational reasoning. The system’s segmentation, error detection, and information retrieval capabilities are extensively evaluated through experiments.

title: MOLE: Metadata Extraction and Validation in Scientific Papers Using LLMs
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP (Findings of EMNLP)
abstract: Metadata extraction is essential for cataloging and preserving datasets, enabling effective research discovery and reproducibility, especially given the current exponential growth in scientific research.While Masader (Alyafeai et al., 2021b) laid the groundwork for extracting a wide range of metadata attributes from Arabic NLP datasets' scholarly articles, it relies heavily on manual annotation.In this paper, we present MOLE, a framework that leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to automatically extract metadata attributes from scientific papers covering datasets of languages other than Arabic.Our schema-driven methodology processes entire documents across multiple input formats and incorporates robust validation mechanisms for consistent output.Additionally, we introduce a new benchmark to evaluate the research progress on this task.Through systematic analysis of context length, few-shot learning, and web browsing integration, we demonstrate that modern LLMs show promising results in automating this task, highlighting the need for further future work improvements to ensure consistent and reliable performance.We release the code 1 and dataset 2 for the research community.

title: MOLE: Metadata Extraction and Validation in Scientific Papers Using LLMs
abstract: Metadata extraction is essential for cataloging and preserving datasets, enabling effective research discovery and reproducibility, especially given the current exponential growth in scientific research. While Masader \cite{alyafeai2021masader} laid the groundwork for extracting a wide range of metadata attributes from Arabic NLP datasets' scholarly articles, it relies heavily on manual annotation. In this paper, we present MOLE, a framework that leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to automatically extract metadata attributes from scientific papers covering datasets of languages other than Arabic. Our schema-driven methodology processes entire documents across multiple input formats and incorporates robust validation mechanisms for consistent output. Additionally, we introduce a new benchmark to evaluate the research progress on this task. Through systematic analysis of context length, few-shot learning, and web browsing integration, we demonstrate that modern LLMs show promising results in automating this task, highlighting the need for further future work improvements to ensure consistent and reliable performance.

title: LLM-Assisted Person Identification in Historical Correspondence
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This presentation is about an LLM-based pipeline for detecting, structuring, and linking person references in the Hammer-Purgstall correspondence as part of a TEI-based digital scholarly edition, and reports preliminary results from a comparative evaluation against human annotators.------------------------- The transformation of historical correspondence from print to TEI-compliant digital editions requires systematic person identification and authority linking—a process traditionally dependent on extensive manual labour and domain expertise. This paper presents a hybrid workflow combining retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with authority database reconciliation to semi-automate person identification while maintaining scholarly standards. Our case study is the correspondence of Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall (1774–1856), with 3,500 transcribed and annotated letters. The corpus was recently converted from a print edition (Höflechner et al. 2018) into TEI-XML digital scholarly edition (Höflechner et al. 2025). While the encoding captures the structural components of the letters, editorial interventions remain largely unaddressed. Person references remain encoded as tags without authority identifiers, while contextual information resides in unstructured editorial notes. This represents a common challenge in correspondence digitization: moving beyond mere structural markup toward what Sahle (2016) defines as “digital editions”, which exploit the capabilities of the digital, rather than replicating the print paradigm. Historical correspondence presents challenges for this transformation. The Hammer-Purgstall collection exemplifies these through variant spellings (Photius vs Photios), abbreviated titles and names (Freih[errn] v[on] Buol ), split annotations ( v[on] Müller ), partial annotations ( Abu‘l-Fida Imad ad-Din Ismail ibn Ali al-Ayubi), and implicit contextual information in editorial notes attached to elements. Our goal is to develop an LLM-based approach to resolve the annotation errors by capturing full names (including forenames and roles), and linking them to authority files. Amid ongoing debates on the role of generative AI in digital scholarship (Pollin et al. 2025), the transformation of print editions into “digital editions” constitutes a primary application area for LLMs in the editorial workflow (Pollin et al. 2024; Strutz 2026; Strutz forthcoming). Unlike rule-based systems, LLMs can apply contextual reasoning and semantic interpretation to make informed judgments based on textual evidence. Our methodology implements a multi-stage RAG pipeline that progressively resolves person references through different matching strategies. tags in TEI-annotated letters are extracted with surrounding textual context. In a first stage, these entries are queried against an existing persons index represented in a vector database, resolving straightforward matches. The system then enters an iterative cycle: unmatched names are submitted to the GND (Gemeinsame Normdatei) via the lobid API, with LLM-based disambiguation leveraging letter context to select among multiple candidates (Strutz 2026). Successfully disambiguated persons are added to the vector database, and remaining persons are re-queried against this expanded index, iterating until resolution falls below a meaningful threshold. At this point, unmatched persons are queried against a vector database of the full correspondence corpus, exploiting cross-letter contextual patterns to identify individuals through co-occurrence and descriptive mentions. Finally, the remaining cases are flagged for human reconciliation. This hybrid architecture addresses critical limitations in existing approaches. Simple string matching fails on variant spellings; pure LLM approaches risk hallucinating authority identifiers; population-based heuristics ignore historical context. By separating RAG retrieval from authority linking and employing LLMs only for contextual disambiguation, we minimize hallucination risks while maximizing computational efficiency and scholarly transparency. We evaluate this workflow through comparative testing across proprietary models (GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4.6) and open-source alternatives (OLMo2-32B-Instruct, Qwen3-14B), addressing sustainability concerns in DH infrastructure. This cross-model comparison contributes to community discussions about balancing performance with long-term reproducibility requirements. This work contributes to emerging editorial practices by demonstrating how generative AI can complement human editorial work in enriching structurally digitized texts with the semantic depth characteristic of genuine digital editions, recognizing that as transformer-based LLMs integrate into digital scholarship, their capabilities and limitations must be critically assessed.

title: Editorial: Generative AI, human authorship and the transformation of scholarly communication
abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools into academic workflows represents a structural transformation in scholarly communication, rather than a transient technological trend (Dwivedi, Malik, Hughes, & Albashrawi, 2024). Similar concerns have been raised in recent editorials in management journals (Arsenyan & Piepenbrink, 2024), which highlight how digital transformation, AI and internationalization pressures are reshaping editorial standards, ethical expectations and scholarly practices (Dwivedi et al., 2023, 2024; Pinochet, Schnaider, & Carvalho, 2025). Unlike conventional software used for editing, formatting or reference management, large language models (LLMs) actively participate in text generation and rhetorical structuring (Brown et al., 2024), thereby challenging long-standing assumptions regarding authorship, intellectual responsibility and research integrity (Dwivedi et al., 2024). This phenomenon reflects what some scholars have characterized as an instant research paradigm, in which GenAI systems potentially conduct multiple steps of the research process simultaneously, raising fundamental questions about scholarly authenticity and human agency in knowledge production.Academic journals are urged to address this new scenario and develop new policies for the use of GenAI tools. Editorial responses to this transformation must engage with the ethical foundations that sustain trust, accountability and transparency in scientific knowledge production (Gatrell, Muzio, Post, & Wickert, 2024). This editorial examines how GenAI reshapes academic writing practices and discusses the ethical boundaries, responsibilities and governance principles required to preserve research integrity. At stake is not only compliance with emerging editorial policies but also the preservation of human authorship as the epistemic condition that sustains interpretation, accountability and legitimacy in scholarly communication.In this context, editorials play a distinctive role in scholarly governance as normative reference points that articulate values, frame ethical expectations and reduce interpretive ambiguity within the scholarly community. By clarifying principles rather than prescribing rigid rules, editorials contribute to a shared ethical understanding among authors, reviewers and editors, addressing the need for discipline-specific guidance, which has become increasingly evident across academic communities (Delios, Li, Schotter, & Vrontis, 2024; Delios, Tung, & Van Witteloostuijn, 2025).Recent reviews of research writing practices indicate that the ethical challenges associated with GenAI are intensified by the absence of harmonized policies across journals and publishers (Okina, 2024). Rather than operating within a coherent normative framework, authors are often confronted with fragmented, ambiguous or incomplete guidance regarding acceptable AI use in academic writing (Ngwenyama & Rowe, 2024). This lack of alignment creates ethical uncertainty and shifts responsibility from institutional governance to individual interpretation, increasing the likelihood of inconsistent disclosure practices and undermining shared standards of academic integrity (Bolaños, Salatino, Osborne, & Motta, 2024).Recent debates in publication ethics have highlighted that the central issue is not whether AI should be used in academic writing, but how, to what extent and under whose responsibility (Dwivedi & Helal, 2026). The presence of hallucinations and AI-generated confident but inaccurate assertions (Thomas, Romasanta, & Pujol Priego, 2026), particularly, threatens the epistemic integrity of academic research, and such errors are especially problematic when AI systems are applied to text analysis and literature synthesis without rigorous human oversight. Evidence from recent systematic and rapid reviews suggests that the ethical dilemma surrounding AI use in academic writing is not whether such tools should be employed but how ethical boundaries are interpreted and operationalized in practice. In the absence of clear editorial guidance, researchers often rely on personal judgment, disciplinary norms or perceived editorial tolerance, leading to uneven ethical reasoning and reinforcing the need for clearer governance structures that support the responsible and transparent use of AI technologies. In this sense, the ethical challenge is not exhausted by asking whether GenAI is present in academic writing. Still, by distinguishing acceptable, sensitive and unacceptable forms of use according to the research stage, the degree of human oversight and the risks posed to intellectual authorship.Viewing it through this lens, ethical engagement with GenAI in academic writing should not be understood as a binary choice between acceptance and prohibition, but as a process of progressive ethical maturation (Delios et al., 2024). What is required, therefore, is not merely procedural compliance but the preservation of cognitive responsibility: human authors must remain the primary agents of framing, interpretation, validation and judgment throughout the scholarly process (Tosi, 2025).As researchers integrate AI tools into scholarly workflows, the central challenge is to develop reflective, responsible and transparent practices that evolve with technological capabilities. Editorial guidance must support this trajectory by encouraging a conscious and proportionate use of AI, rather than treating ethical compliance as a static or purely procedural requirement. This approach acknowledges both the opportunities that AI offers for supporting researchers, particularly non-native English speakers who benefit from language refinement assistance, and the genuine epistemological risks posed by uncritical adoption (Barman, Wood, & Pawlowski, 2024).Good practice guidelines suggest that ethical parameters for AI should not be generic; rather, they should vary with technology and, above all, with the stage of the scientific process in which the tool is applied. This perspective shifts governance away from a binary logic of permit versus prohibit, toward defining proportional uses and safeguards for each phase.AI can contribute to specific tasks in scientific writing, such as identifying research gaps, assisting with content drafting and structuring, extracting data for evidence synthesis, supporting data analysis and interpretation and generating figures and tables (Dwivedi & Helal, 2026). A more precise editorial interpretation also requires recognizing that AI assistance is not ethically uniform. Technical assistance, organizational support and heuristic exploration may be acceptable when explicitly disclosed and critically reviewed. In contrast, substantive substitutions in hypothesis formulation, data interpretation or conclusion writing directly threaten the boundary between assistance and authorship. However, such support must not undermine intellectual authorship: the tool should assist rather than replace the researcher's work, and any AI-assisted text must undergo critical review and content validation, including verification of cited references (Dwivedi & Helal, 2026; Dwivedi et al., 2024).A critical ethical distinction that must be made explicit in editorial policies is the difference between AI-generated and AI-assisted writing. AI-generated writing refers to situations in which AI systems autonomously produce substantial portions of academic texts without meaningful human intellectual control. Such practices raise serious concerns about the attribution of intellectual agency, the erosion of accountability and the misrepresentation of scholarly contributions, particularly when left undisclosed (Gatrell et al., 2024). The fundamental issue is that autonomous AI text generation produces content that, while superficially authoritative, is susceptible to factual errors and misrepresentations (Kulkarni et al., 2024); in extreme cases, it may reference research papers that do not exist or provide incorrect identifiers of unrelated work, presenting what amounts to scholarly hallucinations (Dwivedi et al., 2024).Empirical studies indicate that this distinction is not always consciously perceived by authors (Brown et al., 2024). In many cases, researchers cognitively reframe AI-assisted contributions as extensions of their own thinking, particularly when generative systems are used simultaneously to structure arguments or refine expressions. This cognitive reframing reduces the perceived need for disclosure. It blurs the boundary between assistance and substitution, posing a subtle but significant challenge to traditional notions of authorship and intellectual ownership. Research has demonstrated that human reviewers struggle to reliably distinguish between human-authored and AI-generated abstracts (Kulkarni et al., 2024), further complicating editorial oversight.Ethical analyses consistently emphasize that authorship in scholarly publishing is inextricable from accountability (Hosseini, Rasmussen, & Resnik, 2024). From this perspective, the production of text alone does not constitute authorship unless accompanied by the capacity to assume moral, legal and epistemic responsibility for the content. Because AI systems lack agency, intentionality and accountability, their contributions, regardless of sophistication, cannot meet the normative criteria for scholarly authorship. Scholarly writing is not merely the production of grammatically coherent text; it is an interpretive and moral act through which authors assume responsibility for meaning, evidence and intellectual consequences. Major journal publishers have explicitly articulated this principle; for instance, Science journals have clarified that text generated by ChatGPT or other AI tools cannot be used in scholarly work, nor can such tools produce figures or graphics, and that violations constitute scientific misconduct (Lindebaum & Fleming, 2024).In contrast, AI-assisted writing involves the use of generative systems as supportive tools in human-led research processes (Pinochet, Moreira, Fávero, Santos, & Pardim, 2023). In such cases, AI may contribute to linguistic refinement, structural organization and preliminary drafting (Gatrell et al., 2024). Simultaneously, human authors retain full responsibility for conceptual development, theoretical coherence, methodological rigor and final editorial decisions. From an ethical standpoint, this distinction is fundamental: the acceptability of AI depends less on the technology itself and more on the preservation of human judgment, critical oversight and explicit disclosure (Thomas et al., 2026). This phenomenon has been described as the AI ghostwriter effect (Draxler et al., 2024), referring specifically to AI-assisted authorship rather than fully AI-generated content, in which generative systems support idea formulation or textual organization. At the same time, human authors retain intentionality, judgment and responsibility for the final text, remaining psychologically invisible as external agents. Unlike intentional misconduct, this effect reflects altered perceptions of authorship rather than strategic concealment, suggesting that ethical governance must address not only formal rules but also the cognitive dynamics that shape how AI involvement is interpreted and justified.Beyond individual instances of disclosure failure, a broader systemic risk emerges when GenAI becomes normalized and psychologically invisible in academic writing practices. As AI-mediated structuring, phrasing and ideation become routine, the risk of homogenization in scholarly argumentation, rhetorical patterns and epistemic styles increases. Such normalization may subtly reshape academic discourse, raising concerns not only about authorship and accountability but also about intellectual diversity, originality and the depth of scholarly reasoning. This process may reinforce automation bias and reduce the epistemic vigilance and reflective scrutiny required for rigorous scholarship, especially when scholars begin to rely on fluent AI-generated outputs without sustained verification (Heersmink, 2024; Wong, 2024). Because language models rely on existing literature, heightened attention is needed to avoid the literal reproduction of passages from other authors. This concern is relevant even in the absence of intentional misconduct, as reliance on training corpora may induce textual reuse and unnoticed standardization (Ignjatović & Stevanović, 2023). Recent discussions in the information science and education literature suggest that excessive reliance on GenAI systems may weaken cognitive engagement, critical thinking and creative processes that are central to academic writing (Helal et al., 2025; Kumar & Gunn, 2025; Lindebaum & Fleming, 2024). While generative tools may accelerate drafting and ideation, sustained dependence risks bypassing the reflective, evaluative and iterative stages traditionally associated with scholarly reasoning, raising concerns that extend beyond authorship to the epistemic quality and intellectual depth of academic work.From an editorial standpoint, the ethical acceptability of AI-assisted writing depends on preserving meaningful human control throughout the research process (Thomas et al., 2026). Reviews of editorial policies have indicated that GenAI may be ethically integrated as a support mechanism for language refinement or structural organization, provided that human authors retain responsibility for conceptual framing, methodological decisions and interpretive judgment. This reinforces the principle that ethical evaluation should focus on responsibility and oversight rather than the mere presence of GenAI tools.In practice, transparency is strengthened when authors maintain a minimal provenance record of GenAI assistance (tool name, model/version, date of use and a brief description of prompts or interactions) so that the origins and reliability of AI-assisted passages can be evaluated if questions arise (Herhausen, Ludwig, Abedin, Haque, & De Jong, 2025). Such disclosure is strongest when it identifies not only the tool and model/version used, but also the purpose of use, the degree of intervention and the stage of the manuscript or research process affected, thereby creating conditions for traceability, ethical auditability and informed editorial judgment.This approach acknowledges that prompt engineering and the specific formulation of queries to LLMs significantly influence outputs, making the reproducibility of LLMs essential for scholarly verification (Wobst & Lueg, 2025). For editorial purposes, this differentiation provides a practical and principled framework for evaluating submissions, guiding authors and safeguarding research integrity without impeding legitimate methodological innovations (Herhausen et al., 2025).Within AI-mediated scholarly communication, peer reviewers play a pivotal yet often underarticulated role (Bechky & Davis, 2025). In this evolving landscape, reviewers should be understood not as technological detectors of hidden AI use but as evaluators of coherence, transparency, proportionality and human intellectual responsibility in manuscripts shaped by AI-mediated workflows. Beyond evaluating technical rigor and theoretical contributions, reviewers increasingly serve as interpreters of transparency disclosures and assessors of intellectual coherence in AI-assisted manuscripts. Their role is not to police authorship through technological suspicion but to exercise informed human judgment, contextual sensitivity and ethical discernment, reinforcing the centrality of human oversight within the publication process. This requires reviewers to develop new competencies in recognizing the variable performance profiles of LLMs across different tasks, understanding that AI systems exhibit jagged competencies, where they may perform reliably on certain tasks while failing significantly on others (Thomas et al., 2026).Editorial policies that attempt to ban the use of GenAI in academic writing face three structural limitations. First, such bans are largely unenforceable given the current and foreseeable limitations of AI detection technologies (Andrews, Fainshmidt, & Gaur, 2026). The reliability of detection tools remains contested, and researchers have raised significant concerns about false positives and methodological opacity in AI detection mechanisms. title: NeuroSym-BioCAT: Leveraging Neuro-Symbolic Methods for Biomedical Scholarly Document Categorization and Question Answering
abstract: The growing volume of biomedical scholarly document abstracts presents an increasing challenge in efficiently retrieving accurate and relevant information. To address this, we introduce a novel approach that integrates an optimized topic modelling framework, OVB-LDA, with the BI-POP CMA-ES optimization technique for enhanced scholarly document abstract categorization. Complementing this, we employ the distilled MiniLM model, fine-tuned on domain-specific data, for high-precision answer extraction. Our approach is evaluated across three configurations: scholarly document abstract retrieval, gold-standard scholarly documents abstract, and gold-standard snippets, consistently outperforming established methods such as RYGH and bio-answer finder. Notably, we demonstrate that extracting answers from scholarly documents abstracts alone can yield high accuracy, underscoring the sufficiency of abstracts for many biomedical queries. Despite its compact size, MiniLM exhibits competitive performance, challenging the prevailing notion that only large, resource-intensive models can handle such complex tasks. Our results, validated across various question types and evaluation batches, highlight the robustness and adaptability of our method in real-world biomedical applications. While our approach shows promise, we identify challenges in handling complex list-type questions and inconsistencies in evaluation metrics. Future work will focus on refining the topic model with more extensive domain-specific datasets, further optimizing MiniLM and utilizing large language models (LLM) to improve both precision and efficiency in biomedical question answering.

title: LLMs-based Thematic Analysis of Social Media Deepfakes and its Empirical Parallelism with Deepfake News
venue: Journal of the Association for Information Systems
abstract: This paper discusses deepfakes in social media, a phenomenon that poses a critical challenge to digital trust and information integrity. The deepfakes are improving as technical artifacts, but a cohesive synthesis of the literature is lacking. To address this gap, we conducted a thematic analysis of 109 relevant articles from the literature (2018–2026) that examine the socio-technical implications of deepfakes. Our methodology introduces a rigorous cross-model synthesis through Large Language Models (LLMs). The emerged themes are subsequently mapped onto a corpus of online news articles extracted via GDelt API, using GLDA topic modeling to analogize scholarly findings with real-world insights. The study further identifies critical research gaps in the deepfake domain as it overcommits reactive (forensic detection) and neglects anticipatory (digital literacy) approaches, leading to a Structural Reactivity Gap. This provides the theoretical basis for shifting the deepfake research paradigm from artifact-centric (detecting deepfakes) to agent-centric (understanding deepfakes).

title: Complementary Vulnerabilities: A Systematic Review Comparing Reasoning Failures in Human and LLM Clinical Decision-Making
abstract: Authors and Affiliations Mohsen Amoei. McGill University, Montreal, Quebec, Canada / Mila - Quebec AI Institute, Montreal, Quebec, Canada Elena Guadagno. Harvey E. Beardmore Division of Pediatric Surgery, The Montreal Children's Hospital, McGill University Health Centre, Montreal, Quebec, Canada Dr Dan Poenaru. Harvey E. Beardmore Division of Pediatric Surgery, The Montreal Children's Hospital, McGill University Health Centre, Montreal, Quebec, Canada Review Question What are the distinct reasoning failure patterns exhibited by human clinicians and large language models (LLMs) in clinical decision-making, how do these failure patterns compare across both systems, and to what extent are they complementary, redundant, or orthogonal? Methods Searches Scientific Literature A medical librarian searched the following databases from January 2018 onward: PubMed, MEDLINE (Ovid), Embase (Ovid), and Scopus. The search employed a three-arm strategy: Search A targeted human clinical reasoning errors using terms related to cognitive biases, diagnostic errors, heuristics, and clinical decision-making failures; Search B targeted LLM clinical reasoning evaluation using terms related to large language models, medical benchmarks, AI hallucination, and reasoning failures; Search C targeted direct human-LLM comparative studies using combined terms from both domains. The search strategy used variations in text words found in the title, abstract or keyword fields, and relevant subject headings to retrieve articles examining reasoning failures in clinical decision-making by either human clinicians or large language models. Grey Literature arXiv was searched for preprints related to LLM clinical reasoning evaluation and AI cognitive biases in healthcare. Forward and backward citation searching (snowballing) will be conducted on all included studies. Conference proceedings and dissertation databases will also be searched. Domain Being Studied This systematic review examines clinical reasoning failures in both human clinicians and large language models performing healthcare decision-making tasks. The domain encompasses diagnostic reasoning, treatment planning, triage, and clinical judgment across all medical specialties. Human reasoning failures include cognitive biases (anchoring, confirmation bias, availability heuristic, premature closure), fatigue-related errors, and experience-dependent failures. LLM reasoning failures include hallucination, prompt sensitivity, context window limitations, training data biases, and non-reproducibility. The review specifically focuses on how and why reasoning fails (failure mechanisms) rather than aggregate performance metrics alone. Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria Studies were included if: (1) the study examined clinical reasoning or diagnostic decision-making by human clinicians (physicians, nurses, medical trainees) or large language models (GPT-4, Med-PaLM, LLaMA, and similar); (2) the study analyzed reasoning failures, errors, cognitive biases, or error mechanisms rather than reporting only accuracy metrics; (3) the study was published in English from January 2018 onward; (4) the study was a primary research article, including empirical studies, benchmark evaluations, randomized experiments, observational studies, cross-sectional surveys, or retrospective analyses; (5) for LLM studies, the system evaluated was a transformer-based large language model. Studies were excluded if: (1) the study focused exclusively on non-clinical AI applications (e.g., administrative, scheduling); (2) the study involved only rule-based or traditional machine learning systems without large language models; (3) the study reported only aggregate accuracy, sensitivity, or specificity without characterizing specific failure types or reasoning mechanisms; (4) the study was an editorial, opinion piece, letter, commentary, or conference abstract without primary data; (5) the study was a case report describing individual diagnostic errors without systematic analysis of reasoning mechanisms. Main Outcome(s) The outcomes of this study will focus on (1) developing a unified taxonomy of clinical reasoning failure types classified as human-unique, LLM-unique, or shared between both systems, with characterization of underlying mechanisms for each failure type; (2) assessing the degree of complementarity between human and LLM reasoning failures, measured by the proportion of failure types that are unique to each system versus shared; (3) determining the prevalence of each failure type reported as the percentage of included studies documenting each reasoning failure; and (4) identifying clinical domains and task types most susceptible to each category of reasoning failure. The unified taxonomy refers to a comprehensive classification framework that maps all identified reasoning failure types into three mutually exclusive categories based on convergent evidence from multiple studies. Complementarity will be assessed by examining whether systems show strengths where the other shows weaknesses, supporting collaborative deployment models. Measures of Effect This review uses qualitative thematic synthesis rather than quantitative meta-analysis. The primary measure is the classification of each reasoning failure type into one of three categories: human-unique, LLM-unique, or shared. For each failure type, prevalence will be reported as the percentage of included studies documenting that failure. For shared failures, mechanistic differences between human and LLM manifestations will be described qualitatively. The degree of complementarity will be expressed as the ratio of unique-to-shared failure types across both systems. Additional Outcome(s) These outcomes will explore the broader implications and applications of the comparative failure taxonomy: Mitigation Strategy Effectiveness: Evaluating the effectiveness of reported mitigation strategies (e.g., structured reasoning prompts, cognitive debiasing techniques, retrieval-augmented generation, chain-of-thought prompting) for reducing reasoning failures in each system, and identifying which strategies show cross-system applicability. Complementarity Thesis Evidence: Assessing evidence for or against the complementarity thesis, specifically whether human and LLM reasoning strengths and weaknesses are inversely correlated, supporting collaborative deployment over substitution models in clinical settings. Domain-Specific Vulnerability Mapping: Mapping failure types to specific clinical specialties and task complexity levels to identify which clinical contexts are most and least suitable for human-AI collaborative decision-making. Data Extraction Data will be extracted using a standardized extraction form. The extraction form will be pilot-tested on a sample of 20 studies to ensure clarity and consistency before proceeding with full data extraction. Extracted data will include: standard bibliographic information (author(s), title, year, journal, DOI/PMID), study design, clinical domain and medical specialty, population characteristics (clinician type, experience level, or LLM model evaluated), reasoning failure types identified with definitions provided by the study authors, failure mechanisms described, prevalence or frequency data where reported, mitigation or debiasing strategies evaluated and their effectiveness, and study limitations. Data will be extracted by one reviewer and verified by a second reviewer. Any disagreements will be resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. A Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) Flow Diagram will be created to detail the number of records identified, screened, included, and excluded, as well as the reasons for exclusions. Strategy for Data Synthesis For this systematic review, data from the included studies will be synthesized using thematic synthesis following the approach described by Thomas and Harden (2008). The synthesis proceeds in three stages: (1) line-by-line coding of extracted data to identify reasoning failure types reported in each study, (2) organization of codes into descriptive themes representing distinct failure categories, and (3) generation of analytical themes through cross-domain comparison of human and LLM failure patterns. Failure types will be classified as human-unique, LLM-unique, or shared based on convergent evidence from multiple studies. For shared failure types, the underlying causal mechanisms in humans versus LLMs will be compared to determine whether failures arise from analogous or distinct processes. Quantitative descriptive statistics will summarize the frequency of each failure type across studies, the distribution of studies across clinical domains, the proportion of studies supporting each taxonomy category, and study quality ratings. No statistical meta-analysis of effect sizes is planned due to the heterogeneity of study designs and outcome measures. Results will be presented using narrative synthesis supplemented by summary tables and a taxonomy visualization diagram. The synthesis findings will be reported in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines. Analysis of Subgroups or Subsets Subgroup analyses will be conducted to explore variation in reasoning failure patterns across the following dimensions: (1) Clinical domain: Comparing failure patterns across specialties (e.g., emergency medicine, oncology, radiology, primary care, surgery) to identify domain-specific vulnerabilities in both human and LLM reasoning. (2) LLM model type: Analyzing whether different model architectures (e.g., GPT-4, Med-PaLM, LLaMA, Claude) exhibit different failure profiles, and whether newer models show improvement on specific failure types.
